Printing Houses only provide yields if you have many City-State Friends and Allies, or if you are conducting offensive Spy Missions, otherwise they are a drain on your Gold and a diversion of Production. But, if you intend to work Civil Servant slots they are a key Building, and give increased movement and influence for all your Diplomatic Units and the ability to allow your Diplomatic Units to ignore terrain penalties.

From a single print shop in Mainz, Germany, printing had spread to no less than around 270 cities in Central, Western and Eastern Europe by the end of the 15th century. As early as 1480, it is assumed that "the printed book was in universal use in Europe". By 1500, the printing presses in operation throughout Western Europe had already produced more than twenty million copies. European printing presses of around 1600 were capable of producing 3,600 impressions per workday. By comparison, movable type printing in the Far East, which did not know presses and was solely done by manually rubbing the back of the paper to the page, did not exceed an output of forty pages per day. The rapidity of typographical text production, as well as the sharp fall in unit costs, led to the issuing of the first newspapers which opened up an entirely new field for conveying up-to-date information to the public.

Penitentiaries support the development of new Cities by allowing you use Spy Missions to generate global Food bonuses, and by making new Workers produce improvements faster. They also benefit large, established Cities my making them less susceptible to Spies and allowing them to generate more Military Supply. Both high-population Empires and those with many Cities will appreciate the Empire Size Modifier reduction.

A penitentiary or prison is a facility where people are imprisoned against their will and denied their liberty under the authority of the state, generally as punishment for various crimes. From the late 17th century and during the 18th century, popular resistance to public execution and torture became more widespread both in Europe and in the United States. Imposition of the death penalty for petty crimes, such as theft, was proving increasingly unpopular with the public; many jurors were refusing to convict defendants of petty crimes when they knew the defendants would be sentenced to death. Rulers began looking for means to punish and control their subjects in a way that did not cause people to associate them with spectacles of tyrannical and sadistic violence. They developed systems of mass incarceration, often with hard labor, as a solution. Prisons can also be used as a tool of political repression by authoritarian regimes who detain perceived opponents for political crimes, often without a fair trial or due process; this use is illegal under most forms of international law governing fair administration of justice.

Jails are the earliest Building that interacts with Spies. Both offensively and defensively the Jail improves your edge in the espionage game. In terms of investment, Jails cover their own maintenance cost and adding a small amount of production that eventually pays off the construction costs. However, if you have nearby Quarries you will want to construct jails to set your prisoners to work!

A jail refers to a location where a people charged with crimes may be imprisoned until their trial or simply held for a brief time for public safety. Imprisonment as a penalty was used initially for those who could not afford to pay their fines. Eventually, since impoverished Athenians could not pay their fines, leading to indefinite periods of imprisonment, time limits were set instead. The prison in ancient Athens was known as the desmoterion ("place of chains"). The Romans were among the first to use prisons as a form of punishment rather than simply for detention. A variety of existing structures were used to house prisoners, such as metal cages, basements of public buildings, and quarries. Generally speaking, longer term or indefinite detention was not brought into the mainstream as a punitive measure until much later, mostly owing to the large logistical overhead of managing such sites and the existance of the institution of slavery. Today, locations that hold people for shorter periods of time are usually operated by a local government, in America this would be the county sheriff.

The precise origin of gambling is unknown. It is generally believed that it has been seen in some form or another in almost every society in history. The first known European gambling house, not called a casino although meeting the modern definition, was the Ridotto, established in Venice, Italy, in 1638 by the Great Council of Venice to provide controlled gambling during the carnival season. It was closed in 1774 as the city government felt it was impoverishing the local gentry. Such locations have been famous throughout the Modern era, often featuring in literature as extravagant (or even taboo) settings for tense interpersonal encounters over cards or roulette. From the concept of the house edge to the off-and-on illegality of gambling, casinos have always had a close association with crime and criminality.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]The nature of the casino was to change irreversibly in 1891 when Sittman and Pitt of Brooklyn, New York, developed the first gambling machine. These were primitive mechanical contraptions that often rewarded the player with candy to avoid anti-gambling regulations and because of the computational difficulty of assigning prizes based on rarity. Still, by the 1980s design had advanced considerably, with slot machine manufacturers incorporating microprocessors into their products and programming them to weight particular symbols. Thus the odds of losing symbols appearing on the payline became disproportionate to their actual frequency on the physical reel. Today the gambling industry is worth over $100 Billion, with slot machines averaging about 70% of a standard U.S. casino's income.

Although the Casino generates Gold, its Maintenance Cost is higher, making it a poor investment. However, if you operate an offensive Spy network, then the Gold and Culture flowing from your Agents' daring Missions will make the Casino worth your while. The building further benefits from the Penitentiary gaining Border Growth Points from Spy Missions by also giving yields upon border expansion. At Computers the Maintenance Cost is effectively removed, making the Casino a net positive to any City with the Production to spare.
